::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Operators adapted from prior work.** Plexus re-implements published simulation code
as registered operators: attraction–repulsion and boids from
[ParticleGraph](https://github.com/allierc/ParticleGraph); the slime-mould (Physarum)
agent from [Sebastian Lague's Slime-Simulation](https://github.com/SebLague/Slime-Simulation);
softened self-gravity from Philip Mocz's *Create Your Own N-body Simulation* (2020); the
continuum solver from MLS-MPM (Hu et al. 2018); and the strange attractors from their
originating papers (Lorenz 1963, Rössler 1976, Sprott 1994, …).
:::

Biology is not a single graph.

A graph fixes *one* kind of node and *one* kind of edge — particles and the
forces between them, cells and their contacts, neurons and synapses,
molecular species and reactions. Each existing framework commits to one such
graph and models that layer alone. But a living system is several of these at once, nested inside one
another: particles make up cells, and cells make up tissues and populations.
And every level may be coupled to continuous fields — a morphogen gradient, a
pressure field, a chemical signal — that the discrete entities both shape and
read. Choose any single graph and you capture one slice — the couplings
*between* slices, where much of the biology lives, fall outside it.

Rather than building another domain-specific simulator, Plexus introduces one common
representation built from **five primitives**: **sets** of discrete entities across scales, the
**state** each element carries, **fields** of continuous quantities over space, **maps** — the
index relations between sets, both containment and connection — and **operators** that transform
state along those maps.

State is what makes the objects interchangeable: a particle carrying $\{\text{pos},\text{vel}\}$
and a neuron carrying $\{\text{voltage},\text{calcium}\}$ are the *same* object under different
schemas. And an operator is a **contract**, not a piece of biophysics — `neuron_voltage` names
"membrane state $\to$ its derivative," which Hodgkin–Huxley, Izhikevich, a Neural ODE, or an MLP
all satisfy interchangeably. State moves through just **four operator kinds** — **lateral**
(within a set), **aggregate** (up a map), **broadcast** (down a map), and **exchange** (between
a set and a field) — and a model is a **schedule** that composes them.

Plexus is therefore not another simulator but a typed **intermediate representation** for
biological computation: models written for NEURON, Jaxley, or a connectome GNN compile to the
same sets, states, maps, fields, and operators, and existing simulators become *backends* that
implement one family of operator contracts — Plexus is to a biophysics simulator what LLVM is
to a C compiler.

![The four operators. *Lateral* acts within a set; *Aggregate* and *Broadcast* move across containment $\pi$; *Exchange* pushes to and pulls from a field.](figures/fig_ops.png){width=70% fig-align="center"}

## A language *and* a calculus — two layers that never touch

Plexus is two things at once, kept strictly apart:

- a **language** — a small, declarative *specification* (`spec.yaml`) that names
  the sets, fields, operators, and schedule of a system. This is *what* a living
  system is.
- a **calculus** — the registered operators and the engine that composes and
  integrates them. A simulation is a composition of operators,
  declared as a `Schedule`; in math terms, one tick is the composition
  $\Phi = \mathcal{O}_n \circ \cdots \circ \mathcal{O}_1$, iterated as
  $x_{t+1}=\Phi(x_t)$ and kept differentiable throughout. This is *how* it
  evolves.

Both layers are built from **explicit, named primitives**. And because those
primitives are explicit *and* differentiable, the same language serves
prediction, inverse inference, and the optimization of biological designs alike.

The two meet at exactly one place — the validated spec — and **never touch
directly**. The code owns everything *below* the spec: the registered operators
and the engine that runs them. The language owns everything *above* it: the spec
that names the sets, fields, operators, and schedule of a system.

This separation becomes important the moment the framework is connected to an
**LLM**. The LLM works only in the language layer — it reads, edits, and
generates the spec — and never touches the codebase: it never writes engine code,
and the engine never sees natural language. The spec is the contract between
them: small, typed, and human-auditable.

The practical payoff: a new behaviour is a new *sentence* in the language, not a new program —
so a short natural-language prompt can compile to a running, differentiable simulation with no
engine code written. How that compilation works, and how the contract fails loudly on a bad
spec, is on the **[LLM ↔ registry](methodology.qmd)** page.

## What it looks like

Qualitatively different dynamical systems expressed within the same language. Each
simulation is constructed from the same primitives—sets, state, fields, maps, and
operators—yet gives rise to distinct collective behaviours spanning flocking,
self-organizing networks, self-gravity, and deterministic chaos.

And because every simulation is differentiable, biological designs can be
*optimized*, not just simulated — a foraging colony in a maze, tuned end-to-end by a
UCB search, delivers food roughly **five-fold faster**. See
**[Optimization](optimization.qmd)** for the full runs.

## Read the blueprint

This site distils a working prototype into a single blueprint, in four parts:

- **[The abstraction](abstraction.qmd)** — the missing primitive: a hierarchical
  graph container stated in the language of sets, fields, and four operators.
- **[LLM ↔ registry](methodology.qmd)** — the two-layer contract and the small
  declarative language that lets an LLM drive a registry of operators.
- **[Simulations](experiment.qmd)** — the core operator families as multi-example
  panels (interaction, boids, active matter, slime, MLS-MPM, inverse-square, strange
  attractors).
- **[Optimization](optimization.qmd)** — a foraging colony tuned end-to-end by a
  differentiable UCB search, from a hand-set design to the best found.

A static version with full schematics and glossary is in
[`paper/plexus.pdf`](paper/plexus.pdf).
